First, it changed the way that fixed charges were incorporated into the rates paid by residential customers of the State’s IOUs. It did this by repealing a $10 cap on these charges and instead authorizing the CPUC to use fixed charges for any residential rate schedule, provided that the charges were established on an income- graduated basis, with no fewer than three income thresholds, and that low-income ratepayers would realize a lower average monthly bill without making any chances in usage. Second, it established a Distributed Electricity Backup Assets program through which the CEC would incentivize efficiency upgrades to power generators and new zero- or low-emission technologies at new and existing facilities. The resources funded by this provision are required to be available to respond during an extreme event to support grid reliability. Third, it appropriated $200 million for the CEC to create the Demand Side Grid Support Program. One purpose of this program is to “incentivize dispatchable customer load reduction and backup generation operation as on-call emergency supply and load reduction during extreme events.” Another is to reduce customer net load during extreme events by providing funding for upfront capacity commitments and per- unit reductions. The following parties are eligible for payment: “individual entities”; aggregators of multiple energy customers; and local POUs and load-serving entities (LSEs). SB 846 (Dodd, Chapter 239, Statutes of 2022) – which primarily focused on authorizing the extension of operations for the Diablo Canyon Nuclear Power Plant – also contained two provisions of relevance to load flexibility. In the first of these provisions, SB846 required the CEC, in consultation with the CPUC and the California Independent System Operator (CAISO), “to adopt a goal for load shifting to reduce net peak electrical demand and adjust this target in each biennial integrated energy policy report thereafter.” The CEC was required to set the initial target by June 1, 2023, and to develop that target by considering LBNL’s work for the CPUC (the Phase 3 report, summarized above, was specifically mentioned). This provision of SB846 also requires the CEC to consult with the CPUC and CAISO to “recommend policies to increase demand response and load shifting that do not increase greenhouse gas emissions or increase electric rates.” The second provision of SB846 with relevance to load flexibility funds a Clean Energy Reliability Investment Plan that supports programs and projects that “accelerate the deployment of clean energy resources, support demand response, assist ratepayers, and increase energy reliability.”
